claims.text: The eutectic HEA has an FCC matrix containing dispersed sigma phases.
The FCC and sigma phases possess different electrochemical potentials.
An oxide film forms on the HEA surface during high-speed friction and wear.
Mechanical rupture of the oxide film produces adhesive and abrasive wear.
The potential difference between the FCC and sigma phases causes galvanic corrosion.
Oxide-film formation and rupture occur cyclically at FCC–sigma phase boundaries and repeatedly expose fresh metal.
FCC–sigma interfacial boundaries are preferential sites for localized galvanic corrosion after oxide removal.
Freshly exposed phase-boundary regions undergo galvanic attack because of the inherent potential difference between the FCC and sigma phases.
The coupled oxide-rupture and galvanic-corrosion cycle synergistically accelerates total degradation under simultaneous wear and corrosion.
Elevated temperature accelerates oxidation kinetics in the proposed exposure.
Mechanical wear during corrosive exposure repeatedly ruptures the forming oxide layer.
A 3.5 wt.% NaCl medium supports the proposed galvanic corrosion process.
Relative to an alloy with a stable oxide film or homogenized phase distribution, the tested alloy will have greater total degradation.
The tested alloy will have a higher wear rate because of more frequent oxide-film rupture.
The tested alloy will have a higher corrosion current density because of intensified local galvanic interactions.
The proposed mechanism requires an oxidizing environment, oxide-disrupting wear, and a medium that supports galvanic reactions.
The proposed mechanism may cease to dominate when oxidation kinetics are negligible or mechanical wear is minimal.
Suppressing or stabilizing oxide-film formation should reduce total degradation, wear rate, and corrosion rate.

contradictions.description: The mechanism treats the oxide as protective and attributes increased wear and corrosion to its rupture, yet the intervention and falsification test conflate stabilizing that film with suppressing or minimizing its formation. Stabilization should preserve protection, whereas preventing formation could leave the metal continuously unprotected; they therefore need not produce the same lower-degradation response.

The stated baseline is a different alloy with a stable film or homogenized phase distribution, whereas the experiment compares identical alloy samples after an environmental or surface modification. These are different controls and test different causal factors.
